correspondence.component_scope: Eastern headward channel and upper/middle westward trunk
correspondence.finding: The eastern feeder in the basin-plan hydrography is on the eastern/southeastern side of Minas and runs north/northwest, then west north of the city. The Arequita original Figure 3 resolves its lower approach past Blanes Viale, the San Francisco junction and the connection to Santa Lucía southwest of the Arequita/Cuervos setting. Beyond that junction the selected route matches the mapped westward Santa Lucía corridor through the Paso Roldán, Fray Marcos, San Ramón and Paso Pache settings, ending at the northern Santa Lucía Chico join.
correspondence.limits: The basin overview contains the headward watercourse but does not print a name on every small upper channel. Identification combines ordinary corridor cartography and the local plan’s explicit route description, not a nearest label or basin association. Exact micro-headwater vertices and the precise Campanero/San Francisco name boundary are unestablished.
correspondence.name_scope: Campanero Grande is the supported headward-component name. The shared reach has differing Campanero/San Francisco scope in the two primary publications. Neither is converted into the name of the whole selected system. Río Santa Lucía applies to the downstream named trunk as representative identity.
correspondence.bounded_primary_prose: Minas IAE printed page 12 describes Campanero Grande from south of Camino Paso Espiga near the Maldonado boundary, northwest across that road and Route 8, west then northwest behind Blanes Viale, receiving San Francisco before Santa Lucía. The Arequita publication uses San Francisco for the common lower joining reach.

correspondence.component_scope: Santa Lucía Chico junction through Santa Lucía/Aguas Corrientes to San José junction
correspondence.finding: The selected route turns south below the Santa Lucía Chico junction, passes the 25 de Agosto/Ituzaingó and Santa Lucía town setting, continues through Aguas Corrientes and the Canelón Grande joining sector, then reaches the San José confluence. Basin-plan Figures 3.3, 4.8, 4.9 and 2.20 show the connected main corridor and distinguish northern/eastern reservoir branches.
correspondence.limits: Aguas Corrientes is a material selected impoundment/river passage. No exact impoundment shoreline or point boundary is assigned.
correspondence.name_scope: Representative Santa Lucía trunk. Paso Severino on Santa Lucía Chico and Canelón Grande reservoir are distinct tributary features, not selected lake passages.
correspondence.bounded_primary_prose: The plan’s surface-water description separates Santa Lucía, Santa Lucía Chico, Canelón Grande/Canelón Chico and San José. Table 4-5 specifically identifies the Aguas Corrientes impoundment with Río Santa Lucía.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower estuarine corridor and actual Río de la Plata terminal
correspondence.finding: Below the San José join, the corridor bends through the lower Santa Lucía wetlands toward the Delta del Tigre and Santiago Vázquez mouth setting. The original DINAMA map reproduced as Figure 2.20 resolves the river, adjoining channels, settlements and Río de la Plata shoreline; Figure 3.3 gives the wider receiving-water setting. The selected final eastward/southward approach and terminal bend belong to this estuarine mouth sector rather than to a nearby coastal stream.
correspondence.limits: Generalized mouth-sector correspondence only; no exact bank, individual delta channel, rendered endpoint or coastal vertex agreement claimed.
correspondence.name_scope: Santa Lucía is the representative lower river. Río de la Plata is the receiving waterbody; small delta branches are not independently named here.
correspondence.bounded_primary_prose: Printed pages 30 and 35 explicitly connect the lower Santa Lucía corridor and its delta/island mouth to Río de la Plata west of Montevideo.

finding: The selected head lies in the Paso Buraleo–upper Ñuble setting east of the Nevados de Chillán. DGA describes the Ñuble as originating at the foot of Paso Buraleo, and the municipal map locates this pass at the eastern mountain margin.

The detailed primary hydrographic view shows a continuous natural Río Ñuble headwater channel, receiving Estero Renegado, Estero Los Pajaritos, Quebrada El Chico and Quebrada El Feo, and then Estero Los Tábanos. These are distinct named channels, not alternate names for the whole selected system.

The retained metadata explicitly marks this fragment border_aligned. Much of its northward selected line does not follow the mapped natural Ñuble channel; it cuts or skirts that channel and the Los Tábanos headwater pattern. No separate hydronym is established for this selected non-channel detour.

This is a fully inspected mapped mismatch. The real headwater channels and their receiving Ñuble valley are visible and connected in the same primary map. It is not an unread interval, an unknown lake outlet, or a transfer to an unestablished receiving river. No claim is made that absence from this map proves no small ephemeral channel can ever exist.
correspondence.correspondence: Full corridor inspected; border-aligned modeled detour lacks a matching named natural channel; known surrounding drainage leads to Ñuble.
correspondence.coverage: Headward setting and entire selected fragment inspected in the original MMA upper-corridor view and the separate detailed headwater view.
correspondence.name_scope: Unspecified selected spur; do not assign either Ñuble or Itata uniformly.

finding: The fragment initially links the border-aligned headward detour into the mapped Ñuble valley near the Los Tábanos junction. That first short connector does not itself have a matching named channel on the source map.

The natural Ñuble course is independently visible continuing from its headwater valley through the Los Tábanos sector, north past the Las Minas/Gato tributary setting and the Los Sauces junction, then northwest and west through the San Fabián corridor into the broad central-valley river.

The long selected valley course corresponds at ordinary corridor scale to the Río Ñuble. Overlapping primary views cover the entire intervening middle, not only isolated name labels. The southern Río Cato joins the Ñuble in the lower central-valley reach, with the Río Chillán/Changaral setting near the downstream end and the following fragment.

DGA prose and Table 2.1 distinguish the upper Ñuble–Los Sauces junction, San Fabián, Cato, Chillán and Changaral before the Itata confluence. No selected lake or reservoir passage is required in these viewed corridors.
correspondence.correspondence: Valley reaches supported throughout; initial modeled detour fully observed and excluded from a uniform natural-river naming claim.
correspondence.coverage: Initial detour, upper valley, entire middle course and downstream end inspected using overlapping headwater, upper and middle primary map views.
correspondence.name_scope: Ñuble is supported for the mapped valley, not automatically for the initial detour or downstream Itata.
correspondence.mapped_component_name: Río Ñuble (mapped valley reach after the initial modeled detour)

finding: The selected route continues southwest along the lower Río Ñuble from the Chillán/Changaral junction region toward Confluencia.

The southern Itata branch and eastern Ñuble meet at the selected junction with FIDs14488 and14486. The primary map depicts both approaches and the downstream combined river, while DGA prose explicitly identifies Confluencia as the Ñuble–Itata junction.
The selected end is an actual river confluence, not an ocean mouth or lake outlet. The river name downstream changes to the receiving Itata.
correspondence.coverage: Entire lower Ñuble fragment and actual Itata confluence setting inspected in the overlapping middle and lower primary map views.
correspondence.name_scope: Ñuble for this component; not a whole-system scalar.

finding: Below the Ñuble–Itata confluence, the selected northwestward corridor follows the mapped Río Itata through the coastal-range corridor, with the Chudal and Lonquén tributary settings visible.
The map shows the continuous lower Itata turning westward and broadening into the branched estuarine mouth setting. The entire course between Confluencia and the coast was inspected.

DGA Table 2.1 explicitly carries the lower Itata from the Ñuble junction to Lonquén and then the Pacific Ocean. MMA describes the mouth as the coastal/estuarine wetland between Trehuaco and Coelemu, with Boca Itata and Vegas de Itata on the two municipal sides.
The rendered endpoint reaches the same estuary/Pacific receiving setting at generalized scale. No exact shoreline, bank, seasonal mouth position or individual delta branch agreement is asserted.
correspondence.correspondence: Supported through actual Pacific terminal setting.
correspondence.coverage: Entire lower course, intervening tributary junctions and estuarine/Pacific terminal inspected in the original lower map view and corroborated by primary prose.
correspondence.name_scope: Itata is supported for the receiving lower course and as the bounded receiving-system candidate.

finding: The selected eastern approach is on the mapped Río Cholguán corridor, flowing generally west from the precordillera. DGA describes its headward setting on the western slope of Cerro Calas; the selected fragment is not assumed to include the entire source river.

The viewed route continues through the Cholguán–Huépil formative junction and then turns northwest and north into the upper Itata. DGA explicitly describes Itata as forming near Cholguán station from the eastern Cholguán and southern Huépil.

The MMA hydrographic rendering contains a Río Huépil label on part of the lower formative approach where the DGA prose distinguishes the formers from Itata. This source-label scope difference is retained rather than forcing one scalar over every section.

The entire intervening Itata corridor, including the Danicalqui/Trilaleo setting and the approach to the Diguillín junction, is shown. The selected fragment ends around the Diguillín–Itata junction region and continues through FID14488; it is not a terminal river mouth.
No major selected lake/reservoir transit is shown or required by the available primary geography. No unselected tributary is renamed Itata.
correspondence.coverage: Initial eastern approach, all intervening westward and northward course, Huépil junction and Diguillín junction covered by the south and middle primary map views.
correspondence.name_scope: Multiple river-name scopes; model tributary role does not make the upper Itata a tributary named Ñuble.
correspondence.mapped_component_name: Río Cholguán to upper Río Itata corridor

finding: The selected branch continues north along the Río Itata downstream of the Diguillín confluence, passing the Larqui receiving setting and the minor western tributaries.
Both the northward Itata approach and the eastward Ñuble approach are visible at Confluencia, where this selected tributary fragment ends and FID14486 carries the combined lower Itata.
DGA Table 2.1 explicitly separates the Itata reaches Diguillín–Larqui and Larqui–Ñuble. This establishes the actual terminal receiver without relying only on model connectivity.
correspondence.coverage: Entire Diguillín-to-Ñuble reach and actual terminal confluence inspected in the middle and lower primary views.
correspondence.name_scope: Itata at component scale; not a common name for all modeled mainstem fragments.

correspondence.component_scope: Headward uplands and initial unnamed feeder
correspondence.finding: The selected model begins in the inland southeastern uplands and runs west and northwest. The acquired 97H map shows the corresponding general lake-and-stream setting and an upper Big River course, but the selected initial feeder and its lake or stream links have not been established as one fully read route.
correspondence.correspondence: Partial original-map area reading; initial feeder and material links unresolved.

correspondence.finding: The selected model leaves the southern mapped area northward before bending northwest. No acquired independent original establishes the chosen connecting stream and junctions across this transition.
correspondence.correspondence: Material connector/source coverage gap; no name propagated from either observed end.

correspondence.finding: The retained geometry bends northwest then runs west through the inland part of southern Banks Island. The long central route and its material tributary, lake and channel connections lack an acquired original map.
correspondence.correspondence: Material source gap, not an unresolved naming scope on a completed geographic review.

correspondence.finding: On 98B the named Big River continues west from the eastern sheet edge across low relief, with multiple channels and numerous adjacent ponds. Its broad westward course and coastal approach correspond to the selected western lower corridor. Lennie River is a separately mapped river to the south.
correspondence.correspondence: Supported lower-corridor geographic and cartographic-name correspondence at generalized scale.

correspondence.finding: The lower Big River reaches the Beaufort Sea coastal channel and shore setting in the Siksik Point and Sea Otter Island sector. The source supports the selected coastal outlet at ordinary generalized scale; no inland terminal lake is asserted.
correspondence.correspondence: Supported actual coastal terminal setting at generalized scale; no precise modern branch, bank or mouth vertex claim.

correspondence.component_scope: actual selected headward sector and east-running feeder
correspondence.finding: The selected opening is in the east-running outlet-stream corridor east of Lac Bellanca. Original pixels show connected small channels and ponds toward the Saint-Jean lake/channel setting. The northern arm from Lac Kaministukuakamaht is a separate mapped arm; it is not substituted for the selected western opening.
correspondence.correspondence: bounded headward setting observed; exact feeder hydronym unestablished
correspondence.limits: The source does not establish one scalar river name for the selected western feeder or every intervening lake passage. No natural-source claim for all of Saint-Jean is made.

correspondence.component_scope: upper Saint-Jean lake and river corridor
correspondence.finding: Original pixels show the selected upper corridor joining the lake/channel setting near Lac Mista Uauahk and the Saint-Jean-labeled bend around Mont Kapiskupusteht, then the southward channel alongside the Lac Kapatahkatnahiu Uauahk setting. The large neighboring lake body is not renamed after the river or assumed to be wholly traversed by the selection.
correspondence.limits: Some generalized selected positions lie against the eastern sheet margin; no exact vertex or bank agreement is claimed. Historical map evidence does not establish current official nomenclature.

correspondence.component_scope: Labône–Rapide–Poisset junction sequence and northern middle valley
correspondence.finding: The map shows Labône entering from the west in the upper valley, the southwest-running Saint-Jean valley past a separate Rapide tributary, the major valley turn, and the distinct Poisset tributary toward the southern edge of the sheet. These mapped junction settings correspond to the selected broad upper/middle corridor.

correspondence.limits: Tributary names apply to their own mapped branches and do not become aliases for the selected mainstem.

correspondence.component_scope: southern middle corridor and stage-fragment junction
correspondence.finding: The retained route continues south of the acquired sheet, changes direction through the southern middle corridor and reaches the FID9324 junction. Original cartography for this continuation was not acquired.
